| [LIT-232](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-232.md) v2 | Knowledge Sheaves: A Sheaf-Theoretic Framework for Knowledge Graph Embedding | Gebhart, Hansen and Schrater (2021; AISTATS 2023), [ARXIV-2110.03789](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.03789). A knowledge-graph embedding is a cellular sheaf of vector spaces on the schema graph, with restriction maps per relation type, plus a 0-cochain of its pullback to the knowledge graph. The summed Structured Embedding score is the sheaf Laplacian form, and TransE, TransR and RotatE are special cases; bilinear models are not. Since the zero cochain is always a section, training needs negatives and a margin. Composite multi-hop queries are scored without extra training by harmonic extension, a Schur complement, which beats naive TransE summation on ip and pi queries in untuned experiments. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-843](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-843.md)) in full; worth reading as the clean dictionary between coboundary-type knowledge-graph scores (Structured Embedding, TransE, TransR, RotatE) and cellular sheaves on the schema, with the summed score as a sheaf Laplacian form and multi-hop queries scored by harmonic extension, a Schur complement. Read it knowing that bilinear models fall outside it, that the zero cochain is always a section so all content is in the contrastive margin, that "approximate global section" means only small Laplacian energy, and that the experiments are preliminary, untuned and well below query-embedding baselines. It shares the word "sheaf" with the contextuality line and nothing else of substance. The account is [THEORY-299](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-299.md). |
| [LIT-262](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-262.md) v2 | The Geometry of Information Retrieval | van Rijsbergen (2004), DOI-10.1017/CBO9780511543333. The book recasts IR's vector-space, probabilistic and logical models in one Hilbert-space language. Documents are state vectors. Relevance and aboutness are Hermitian observables that need not commute. Subspaces carry a non-distributive logic whose conditional is shown to be a Stalnaker conditional equal to the Sasaki hook (ch. 5). Gleason's theorem makes tr(ρP) the probability of a subspace, which ch. 6 uses to rewrite cosine matching, cluster representatives, relevance and pseudo-relevance feedback, dynamic clustering and ostensive retrieval. It is a proposed language, not a tested model: no experiment is reported, and its "content hypothesis" that the probability of a concept is cos²θ is argued, not tested. | Active — read in full 2026-09-27 ([NOTE-239](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-239.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of the Hilbert-space (quantum-probability) programme in IR. It is short, self-contained and mathematically careful at the level it works at, and its ch. 5 proof that the subspace conditional is a Stalnaker conditional and its ch. 6 trace-formula recastings of standard IR operations are the parts to take away. Read it as a language, not as evidence: it reports no experiment, and every IR payoff it names is a reformulation or a research direction. |
| [LIT-269](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-269.md) v2 | Attention Approximates Sparse Distributed Memory | Bricken & Pehlevan (2021), [ARXIV-2111.05498](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05498). Kanerva's SDM read weights each stored pointer by the number of neurons in the intersection of two Hamming balls of radius d. The paper shows that this weight is roughly log-linear in Hamming distance for close patterns. As a result, with L²-normalised vectors and a regression-fitted β, softmax attention reproduces SDM's retrieval behaviour on random and learnt-projection data (App. B.7). Two things are weaker than they look. The analytic derivation (App. B.2, Eqs. 16–21) gets the exponent wrong: by my recomputation its β is ≈2–2.5× too small. The biological case is Kanerva's 1988 cerebellar mapping, restated rather than re-argued. It also needs r = 2⁶⁴ ≈ 1.8×10¹⁹ neurons in the Attention setting, which the paper itself calls "biologically implausible" (App. B.5). | Active — read in full 2026-09-27 (NOTE-242); worth reading as the clearest statement of the SDM–attention correspondence. Its exact circle-intersection formula and its eight-algorithm convergence comparison are the parts to take away. Treat its analytic exponential derivation, its GPT-2 "confirmation" and its cerebellar implementation of attention as argument, not demonstration. |

| [LIT-921](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-921.md) v2 | Sparse Distributed Memory and Related Models | Kanerva (1992), RIACS TR 92.10, in Hassoun (ed.) 1993. SDM restated as a matrix memory, with the RAM as its zero-radius case, and related to correlation-matrix memories, feed-forward nets, the cerebellar cortex and the models of Marr and Albus. For uniform random data and exact cues it gives bit fidelity, the optimal activation p = (2MT)^−1/3 and a capacity near a tenth of the hard locations. Also held in the anthology as [ANTH-LIT-669](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/blob/main/record/literature.d/LIT-669.md). | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-779](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-779.md)) in full; worth reading as the compact statement of sparse distributed memory in matrix form, with the ordinary RAM as its zero-radius special case and a simple signal-to-noise analysis: fidelity Φ(ρ) with ρ² = pM/[1 + pT(1 + p²M)], best at p = (2MT)^−1/3, and capacity near a tenth of the hard locations at fidelity 0.999. Read it knowing that every number assumes uniform random data and exact retrieval cues, that the noisy-cue case and the critical distance are not analysed here, and that it relates SDM to the Hopfield net only through a cited capacity comparison. |
| [LIT-928](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-928.md) v2 | Sparse Distributed Memory | Kanerva (1988), MIT Press. An associative memory in a high-dimensional binary space, addressed by content: a pattern is written to every hard location within a radius of its address and read back from the locations within that radius of a cue. Iterated reads converge on a stored pattern only from cues within a critical distance of it. Also held in the anthology as [ANTH-LIT-666](https://github.com/dmarx/anthology-of-the-sota/blob/main/record/literature.d/LIT-666.md). Not read here. | Unavailable — searched 2026-10-14 for a lawful full text, none reached, so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The book has no DOI; the MIT Press page and MIT Press Direct returned Cloudflare 403 checks, and no open-access edition was found; the Internet Archive has no scan of the book; NASA's Technical Reports Server holds Kanerva's public-domain RIACS and Stanford reports on SDM, which are different works (LIT-921 is one of them). What the book says about cues beyond the critical distance, which CLAIM-180 leans on, is therefore still unchecked here. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |

As paraphrased, the abstract says that adding terms to short queries by ad hoc feedback improves retrieval, that the authors refine the set of documents feedback is drawn from, first with manually formulated Boolean filters with proximity constraints and then with a fully automatic method based on term co-occurrence, and that this "often prevents the query drift caused by blind expansion", improving average precision and precision in the top twenty documents, with the automatic method competitive with the best manual one at little added cost. So the paper uses the term query drift and places its cause in blind (pseudo-relevance) expansion; that the mechanism is non-relevant documents in the top-ranked feedback set, the collections used and the sizes of the gains are not confirmed and need the full text.
